clinicalPearls: The cholinergic toxidrome combines muscarinic features summarised as SLUDGE (salivation, lacrimation, urination, defecation, gastrointestinal distress, emesis) with nicotinic effects
The most life-threatening features are the 'killer Bs': bronchorrhoea, bronchospasm and bradycardia causing respiratory failure
A garlic or solvent-like odour and a history of agricultural, pesticide or occupational exposure support the diagnosis
Nicotinic overstimulation produces muscle fasciculations, weakness and, later, paralysis, while central effects cause agitation, seizures and coma
Carbamate inhibition of cholinesterase is reversible and generally shorter-lived than organophosphate poisoning, which can become irreversible after enzyme 'ageing'
Management centres on aggressive antimuscarinic therapy with atropine titrated to drying of secretions, plus an oxime reactivator for organophosphates, with airway protection paramount
An intermediate syndrome of proximal and respiratory muscle weakness can appear one to four days later, and delayed peripheral neuropathy may follow certain agents
Decontamination with removal of clothing and skin washing protects both patient and staff, who should wear protective equipment
reference.pathophysiology: Organophosphates and carbamates inhibit acetylcholinesterase, preventing the breakdown of acetylcholine at muscarinic, nicotinic and central synapses. The resulting accumulation of acetylcholine overstimulates cholinergic receptors, producing the mixed muscarinic and nicotinic cholinergic crisis. Organophosphate-enzyme bonds can undergo 'ageing', becoming permanent and refractory to oxime reactivation, whereas carbamate inhibition spontaneously reverses. Excess cholinergic activity at the neuromuscular junction first causes fasciculations, then depolarising blockade and weakness, while central accumulation drives seizures and depressed consciousness.
additionalDifferentials: Carbamate versus organophosphate agent (affecting reversibility and oxime use)
Nerve agent exposure in a mass-casualty or deliberate setting
Acute pulmonary oedema or asthma from another cause
Other causes of cholinergic-appearing crisis such as pyridostigmine excess
additionalInvestigations: Red-cell (acetyl) cholinesterase and plasma (butyryl) cholinesterase activity to support diagnosis and monitor recovery
Arterial blood gas and continuous oxygen saturation to detect respiratory failure
Electrocardiogram for bradyarrhythmias and QT prolongation
Serum electrolytes, glucose and renal function
Chest radiograph for aspiration or pulmonary oedema
Serial neuromuscular assessment for intermediate syndrome
redFlags: Copious bronchorrhoea and bronchospasm threatening the airway
Progressive muscle weakness or respiratory failure suggesting intermediate syndrome
Inadequate response to escalating antimuscarinic therapy
reference.prognosis: With early airway control, adequate atropinisation and oxime therapy, many patients recover fully, though severe poisoning, delayed presentation or intermediate syndrome may require prolonged ventilation; mortality is driven mainly by respiratory failure and aspiration.
pitfalls: Under-dosing atropine and failing to titrate to clearing of bronchial secretions
Neglecting staff and rescuer decontamination, risking secondary exposure
Missing the delayed intermediate syndrome after apparent recovery
Relying on a single cholinesterase measurement rather than trends
Assuming carbamate poisoning is always trivial and omitting close respiratory monitoring
management: Decontaminate by removing contaminated clothing and washing the skin, using staff personal protective equipment to prevent secondary exposure
Protect the airway and give high-flow oxygen and mechanical ventilation for respiratory failure and bronchorrhoea
Administer antimuscarinic therapy with atropine titrated to drying of pulmonary secretions and reversal of bradycardia as the central pillar
Give an oxime reactivator (pralidoxime) for organophosphate poisoning, before enzyme ageing, to reverse nicotinic effects
Control seizures and agitation with benzodiazepines (diazepam)
Monitor in intensive care with serial cholinesterase activity and vigilance for the delayed intermediate syndrome requiring prolonged ventilation
Provide supportive care and avoid contraindicated agents such as depolarising neuromuscular blockers
